title: Time-lapse digital cameras reveal contrasting environmental controls of leaf phenology in different caatinga physiognomies
authors: Marques AML; Ramos DM; Morellato LPC; Dexter KG; Alberton B; Coutinho IAC
summary: Four years of phenocamera observations compared leaf dynamics in carrasco and crystalline Caatinga communities. Precipitation and temperature influenced both physiognomies, but crystalline Caatinga was more sensitive to rainfall irregularity while carrasco showed more stable growing seasons.

title: The Coexistence of Trees, Shrubs, and Grasses Creates a Complex Picture of Land Surface Phenology in Dry Tropical Ecosystems
authors: Koolen SP; Godlee JL; Alberton B; Ramos DM; Moura MSB; Morellato LPC; Dexter KG
summary: This study compared MODIS and phenocamera vegetation indices across four seasonally dry tropical sites. Fine-resolution cameras revealed distinct phenological behavior among trees, shrubs, and grasses that was obscured in coarser satellite observations.

title: Scale matters: Spatial resolution impacts tropical leaf phenology characterized by multi-source satellite remote sensing with an ecological-constrained deep learning model
authors: Song G; Wang J; Zhao Y; Yang D; Lee CKF; Guo Z; Detto M; Alberton B; Morellato P; Nelson B; Wu J
summary: This study quantified how satellite spatial resolution affects tropical leaf-phenology monitoring. An ecologically constrained deep-learning model showed decreasing accuracy from PlanetScope to Sentinel-2 and Landsat-8, with finer imagery better capturing canopy deciduousness and phenological diversity.

title: An ecologically-constrained deep learning model for tropical leaf phenology monitoring using PlanetScope satellites
authors: Wang J; Song G; Liddell M; Morellato P; Lee CKF; Yang D; Alberton B; Detto M; Ma X; Zhao Y; Yeung HCH; Zhang H; Ng M; Nelson BW; Huete A; Wu J
summary: This study developed an index-guided, ecologically constrained autoencoder to estimate canopy deciduousness from high-resolution PlanetScope imagery. Evaluation across 16 tropical forest sites showed strong agreement with WorldView-2 and phenocamera observations from patch to ecosystem scales.

title: Monitoring immediate post-fire vegetation dynamics of tropical mountain grasslands using phenocameras
authors: Alberton B; Alvarado ST; da Silva Torres R; Fernandes GW; Morellato LPC
summary: This study evaluated phenocameras for tracking immediate regrowth and short-term recovery after fire across four campo rupestre vegetation types in Serra do Cipó. Camera-derived greenness and growing-season metrics captured contrasting recovery dynamics and indicated ecosystem recovery by the third post-fire year.

title: Multiscale phenology of seasonally dry tropical forests in an aridity gradient
authors: Ramos DM; Andrade JM; Alberton BC; Moura MSB; Domingues TF; Neves N; Lima JRS; Souza R; Souza E; Silva JR; Espírito-Santo MM; Morellato LPC; Cunha J
summary: Phenocamera and MODIS time series were compared across seven Caatinga sites along an aridity gradient. Camera-calibrated thresholds improved estimates of growing-season transitions, while rainfall variability influenced greening timing and vegetation productivity.

title: Relationship between tropical leaf phenology and ecosystem productivity using phenocameras
authors: Alberton B; Martin TCM; Da Rocha HR; Richardson AD; Moura MSB; Torres RS; Morellato LPC
summary: This comparative study linked phenocamera-derived leaf phenology with eddy-covariance estimates of gross primary productivity across Caatinga, Cerrado, and Atlantic Forest sites. Camera indices tracked productivity well, while water and light limitation varied among biomes.

title: A Change-Driven Image Foveation Approach for Tracking Plant Phenology
authors: Silva E; da Silva Torres R; Alberton B; Morellato LPC; Silva TSF
summary: This study proposed a change-driven image-foveation method that preserves higher resolution in phenologically relevant regions while reducing detail elsewhere. Validation with vegetation image sequences demonstrated storage savings while retaining information needed for phenology tracking.

title: Leafing Patterns and Drivers across Seasonally Dry Tropical Communities
authors: Alberton B; da Silva Torres R; Sanna Freire Silva T; da Rocha HR; Moura MSB; Morellato LPC
summary: This multi-site study used phenocamera time series to compare leafing seasons in Caatinga and three Cerrado communities. Water availability was the main constraint in Caatinga, whereas day length was more influential across the Cerrado sites.

title: RadialPheno: A tool for near-surface phenology analysis through radial layouts
authors: Mariano GC; Alberton B; Morellato LPC; da Silva Torres R
summary: This software note presented RadialPheno, an R Shiny tool that uses radial layouts to visualize cyclical phenocamera time series. The tool supported comparisons among individuals, species, communities, years, and field- versus camera-derived leaf phenology.

title: Leafing patterns and leaf exchange strategies of a cerrado woody community
authors: Camargo MGG; de Carvalho GH; Alberton BC; Reys P; Morellato LPC
summary: Seven years of observations were used to characterize leaf exchange strategies and growing-season timing in a woody Cerrado community. Leaf fall peaked in the dry season, leaf flushing in the dry-to-wet transition, and interannual climate variation affected community deciduousness.

title: The deadly route to collapse and the uncertain fate of Brazilian rupestrian grasslands
authors: Fernandes GW; Barbosa NPU; Alberton B; Barbieri A; Dirzo R; Goulart F; Guerra TJ; Morellato LPC; Solar RRC
summary: This study assessed threats to Brazilian rupestrian grasslands from mining, land-use change, inadequate conservation policy, and climate change. Scenario models projected severe future habitat losses, with consequences for biodiversity and ecosystem services.

title: Fusion of time series representations for plant recognition in phenology studies
authors: Faria FA; Almeida J; Alberton B; Morellato LPC; da Silva Torres R
summary: This study represented phenological time series as recurrence plots and combined them with visual rhythms for plant recognition. The two representations captured complementary information, and classifier fusion improved fine-grained species classification.

title: Linking plant phenology to conservation biology
authors: Morellato LPC; Alberton B; Alvarado ST; Borges B; Buisson E; Camargo MGG; Cancian LF; Carstensen DW; Escobar DFE; Leite PTP; Mendoza I; Rocha NMWB; Soares NC; Silva TSF; Staggemeier VG; Streher AS; Vargas BC; Peres CA
summary: This perspective examined how phenology can inform conservation biology, including the management of climate-driven mismatches, land-use change, fire, invasive species, and restoration. It also highlighted long-term records and emerging monitoring technologies such as satellites, drones, and digital cameras.

title: Modeling plant phenology database: Blending near-surface remote phenology with on-the-ground observations
authors: Mariano GC; Morellato LPC; Almeida J; Alberton B; Camargo MGG; da Silva Torres R
summary: This article described a database that integrates direct field observations, phenocamera indices, environmental measurements, and plant traits. Developed within the e-Phenology project, the system supports management and analysis of complex tropical phenology time series.

title: Phenological visual rhythms: Compact representations for fine-grained plant species identification
authors: Almeida J; dos Santos JA; Alberton B; Morellato LPC; da Silva Torres R
summary: This article encoded phenological time series as compact visual rhythms and evaluated image descriptors for fine-grained plant identification. The representation achieved high species-recognition accuracy while reducing storage and processing requirements for long-term phenocamera data.

title: PhenoVis – A tool for visual phenological analysis of digital camera images using chronological percentage maps
authors: Leite RA; Schnorr LM; Almeida J; Alberton B; Morellato LPC; da Silva Torres R; Comba JLD
summary: This article presented PhenoVis, a visual-analytics tool for exploring phenocamera image collections. Chronological percentage maps and similarity rankings helped identify seasonal patterns, compare years, and detect phenological events and outliers beyond simple average greenness curves.

title: Time series-based classifier fusion for fine-grained plant species recognition
authors: Faria FA; Almeida J; Alberton B; Morellato LPC; Rocha A; da Silva Torres R
summary: This work evaluated phenological classifiers derived from RGB time series and combined complementary classifiers for fine-grained plant recognition. The fusion framework improved discrimination among Cerrado species with similar leaf functional strategies.

title: Unsupervised Distance Learning for Plant Species Identification
authors: Almeida J; Pedronette DCG; Alberton BC; Morellato LPC; da Silva Torres R
journal: IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Applied Earth Observations and Remote Sensing
summary: This study proposed an unsupervised, rank-based distance-learning method for retrieving similar phenological time series and identifying plant species. Combining multiple time-series signals improved retrieval precision relative to pairwise similarity measures.

title: Deriving vegetation indices for phenology analysis using genetic programming
authors: Almeida J; dos Santos JA; Miranda WO; Alberton B; Morellato LPC; da Silva Torres R
summary: This study introduced a genetic-programming framework to derive vegetation indices from phenocamera imagery. Tests using Cerrado plant time series showed that learned combinations of color information characterized species-level leaf phenology more accurately than conventional indices alone.

title: Applying machine learning based on multiscale classifiers to detect remote phenology patterns in Cerrado savanna trees
authors: Almeida J; dos Santos JA; Alberton B; da Silva Torres R; Morellato LPC
summary: This study combined color and texture information from daily phenocamera images with multiscale machine-learning classifiers. The approach distinguished leaf phenology patterns among Cerrado tree species and supported automated identification of individuals and functional groups.

title: Using phenological cameras to track the green up in a cerrado savanna and its on-the-ground validation
authors: Alberton B, Almeida J,  Helm R,  Torres R.S, Menzel A, Morellato LPC
summary: Digital cameras are reliable tool to capture leaf changes in cerrado vegetation. Three leaf exchange strategies were depicted from the species’ green color change. On-the-ground phenology validated the greening patterns and leaf functional groups
